channels.name: Nathan Lambert

channels.name: AI Engineer

channels.name: Caleb Writes Code

channels.name: Andrej Karpathy

channels.name: 3Blue1Brown

channels.name: Jeremy Howard (fast.ai)

channels.name: Welch Labs

channels.name: Sebastian Raschka
channels.why: Author of 'Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)'; code-along LLM lectures and research summaries.

channels.name: bycloud
channels.why: Quick, research-literate breakdowns of new AI papers (reasoning, MoE, optimizers, inference).

channels.name: Caltech CS156

channels.name: Unsupervised Learning (Jacob Effron)
channels.why: Long interviews with AI founders and researchers on what is really working.

channels.name: ETH Zurich CVG
channels.why: Marc Pollefeys' lab: 3D vision, SLAM and geometry research talks and demos.

channels.name: IBM Technology
channels.why: Lightboard explainers of AI concepts (RAG, agents, embeddings, fine-tuning) in 5 to 15 minutes. Only AI-related videos are kept.

channels.name: CS50 (Harvard)

channels.name: MIT OpenCourseWare

channels.name: Google DeepMind
channels.why: AlphaGo, The Thinking Game, the David Silver RL course and research explainers from the lab itself.

channels.name: Harvard Stat 110
channels.why: Joe Blitzstein's Statistics 110: probability taught through stories and intuition, the probability foundation for machine learning.

channels.name: Umar Jamil
channels.why: Line-by-line PyTorch implementations of transformers, LLaMA, Stable Diffusion and Flash Attention; among the most rigorous from-scratch channels on YouTube.

channels.name: Yannic Kilcher
channels.why: Long, technically serious paper walkthroughs from Attention Is All You Need through modern LLM work, with real critique rather than summary.

channels.name: Machine Learning Street Talk
channels.why: Long-form, adversarial interviews with researchers on generalization, reasoning and AI risk; high conceptual density and no marketing gloss.

channels.name: Dwarkesh Patel
channels.why: Meticulously prepared interviews with the people building frontier AI (Sutskever, Amodei, Hassabis); unusually substantive for the format.

channels.name: Luis Serrano Academy

channels.name: Artem Kirsanov

channels.name: Algorithmic Simplicity

channels.name: Robert Miles AI Safety
channels.why: The clearest on-ramp to AI alignment concepts — specification gaming, reward hacking, mesa-optimization — without diluting them.

channels.name: Jia-Bin Huang
channels.why: University of Maryland vision professor explaining LLM serving, quantization, distributed training and vision architectures in depth.

channels.name: Julia Turc
channels.why: Deep, mathematically careful explainers of LoRA, quantization, mixture-of-experts and the LLM inference stack from an AI researcher.

channels.name: Mutual Information
channels.why: Polished theory explainers on bias-variance, information theory and reinforcement learning that show the math rather than hand-waving it.

channels.name: Steve Brunton
channels.why: SVD, PCA, regression and data-driven methods taught with real mathematical care; the engineering foundation underneath applied ML.

channels.name: Hamel Husain
channels.why: Practitioner-grade education on LLM evals, RAG evaluation and when to fine-tune; the material teams actually need to ship reliable systems.

channels.name: Simon Willison
channels.why: Clear, demo-driven talks on LLM tooling, prompt injection and agent workflows from a prolific practitioner.

channels.name: Sasha Rush
channels.why: Cornell NLP professor; interactive tutorials and lectures on transformers, linear attention, state-space models and LLM systems.

channels.name: Jason Liu
channels.why: Practical, experience-backed talks on RAG, evals and agent reliability from a well-known AI engineer.

channels.name: Anthropic
channels.why: Research talks and explainers from the lab behind Claude, especially mechanistic interpretability, alignment and model behavior.

channels.name: Hugging Face
channels.why: Workshops, journal clubs and course material on transformers, agents and open-model fine-tuning.

channels.name: GPU MODE
channels.why: A lecture series on GPU kernels, CUDA, Triton and attention optimization that goes deeper than almost any university course.

channels.name: Aleksa Gordić (The AI Epiphany)
channels.why: Detailed LLM paper walkthroughs and interviews with model authors (LLaMA, Qwen), plus from-scratch implementation streams.

channels.name: Edan Meyer
channels.why: Research-level reinforcement-learning and LLM explainers grounded in papers and his own experiments.

channels.name: sentdex
channels.why: The Neural Networks from Scratch series is a classic; now mixes practical ML and robotics builds with AI commentary.

channels.name: CodeEmporium
channels.why: Concise, well-animated architecture explainers for transformers, CNNs and segmentation models.

channels.name: Computerphile
channels.why: University of Nottingham academics explaining CS and AI fundamentals with unusual clarity.

channels.name: Arxiv Insights
channels.why: Accessible paper explainers on reinforcement learning, VAEs and AlphaFold; slower cadence but solid conceptual grounding.

channels.name: Latent Space
channels.why: Technical AI-engineering podcast with builders and researchers; strong on how real LLM systems are designed and shipped.

channels.name: Cognitive Revolution
channels.why: Long interviews on AI safety, post-training and research strategy; more substance than typical news podcasts.

channels.name: Vizuara

channels.name: Trelis Research
channels.why: Practical, detailed fine-tuning and voice-AI tutorials with code, configurations and evaluation.

channels.name: Sam Witteveen

channels.name: ritvikmath
channels.why: Whiteboard-clear data-science and statistics explanations, from gradient descent to Bayesian methods and time series.

channels.name: Normalized Nerd

channels.name: Lex Fridman

channels.name: CampusX

channels.name: Daniel Bourke

channels.name: Aladdin Persson
channels.why: Clean PyTorch implementations of transformers, YOLO and detection models, plus paper reviews.

channels.name: Shaw Talebi
channels.why: Clear AI-engineering walkthroughs on RAG, fine-tuning and agents, with an emphasis on real deployments.

channels.name: Dave Ebbelaar
channels.why: No-hype, end-to-end AI agent and RAG tutorials that include production concerns rather than toy demos.

channels.name: James Murdza

channels.name: Brandon Rohrer
channels.why: Veteran data scientist whose visual, first-principles explanations of CNNs, RNNs and transformers are exceptionally clear.

channels.name: Dr. Florent Poux
channels.why: Deep 3D and point-cloud AI tutorials with real code; niche but rigorous.

channels.name: hu-po
channels.why: Long, technical paper deep dives on diffusion, RLHF and multimodal models.

channels.name: Ferdinand Mom
channels.why: Distributed-training tutorials and paper walkthroughs (tensor parallel, DiLoCo) at a level few channels attempt.

channels.name: Abhishek Thakur
channels.why: Search and RAG fundamentals (BM25, hybrid search, reciprocal rank fusion) explained by a Kaggle Grandmaster.

channels.name: Machine Learning with Phil

channels.name: Jeff Heaton
channels.why: Veteran ML instructor covering ensembles, AutoML and deep learning with working code.

channels.name: Valerio Velardo (The Sound of AI)
channels.why: The best structured audio and music AI curriculum on YouTube: DSP, neural TTS, voice cloning and music generation.

channels.name: DataTalksClub
channels.why: Free, cohort-style LLM Zoomcamp and MLOps courses with full lecture material and real projects.

channels.name: Stanford Online
channels.why: Full Stanford courses — CS229, CS231N, CS224N, CS234 — taught by the people who built the field.

channels.name: DeepLearningAI
channels.why: Andrew Ng's courses and practitioner short courses on ML, deep learning, prompting and agents.

channels.name: mathematicalmonk
channels.why: Rigorous, compact lectures on ML, probability and information theory; older but mathematically precise.

channels.name: Pieter Abbeel
channels.why: Berkeley CS294-158 deep unsupervised learning lectures: autoregressive models, diffusion and self-supervised learning.

channels.name: Simons Institute

channels.name: Neel Nanda
channels.why: Mechanistic interpretability from one of the field's leading practitioners: transformer circuits, induction heads and live paper reviews.

channels.name: Alfredo Canziani
channels.why: NYU deep learning course with Yann LeCun: energy-based models, self-supervised learning and full graduate rigor.

channels.name: Kilian Weinberger
channels.why: Cornell CS4780 machine learning lectures: SVMs, kernels, bagging and boosting explained with precision.

channels.name: Outlier

channels.name: Jay Alammar

channels.name: Neural Breakdown with AVB

fNk_zzaMoSs: HN's go-to recommendation for learning linear algebra intuition, repeatedly credited with making concepts click and complementing textbooks.

fNk_zzaMoSs.summary: The first chapter of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Linear Algebra series, introducing vectors with animated geometric visuals. It begins a series that builds intuition for linear algebra from the basics.
fNk_zzaMoSs.quote: the most welcoming and informative introduction to the topic I've ever seen

VMj-3S1tku0: HN treats it as the best starting point for really understanding backprop and neural nets, because Karpathy explains the why with intuition and builds everything in code.

VMj-3S1tku0.summary: Andrej Karpathy's first Neural Networks: Zero to Hero lecture, which builds micrograd, a tiny autograd engine, from scratch in Python. It explains backpropagation and neural network training step by step, assuming only basic Python and some high-school calculus.
VMj-3S1tku0.quote: It's especially useful because he explains the why and provides intuitive explanations instead of just talking about the what and how.

aircAruvnKk: HN treats it as the standard first stop for learning neural networks, praised for making the math intuitive.

aircAruvnKk.summary: 3Blue1Brown's first chapter on deep learning explains what neurons and layers are and the math underlying a basic neural network, using handwritten digit recognition with visual animations.
aircAruvnKk.quote: the visualisations and explanations of the math/concepts are so amazing

ZK3O402wf1c: It is HN's default recommendation for learning linear algebra, praised for Strang's teaching and for building real understanding useful in machine learning.

ZK3O402wf1c.summary: The first lecture of Gilbert Strang's MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra course, covering the geometry of linear equations. It opens a full 35-lecture university course.
ZK3O402wf1c.quote: I highly recommend the MIT 18.06 open course on linear algebra - the lectures are first rate.

7Pq-S557XQU: HN has recommended it for a decade as the standard explainer on automation and unemployment, though skeptics later cite it as an example of overconfident predictions.

7Pq-S557XQU.summary: CGP Grey's video "Humans Need Not Apply" argues that automation will make a large part of the workforce economically obsolete, much as engines did for horses. It surveys robots and software replacing both physical and mental labor.
7Pq-S557XQU.quote: Excellent video on the subject: CGPGrey - Humans Need Not Apply

WXuK6gekU1Y: HN commenters call it a moving, well-made human story about AI and Go that works for non-technical viewers and does not date.

WXuK6gekU1Y.summary: Feature-length documentary following DeepMind's AlphaGo program as it prepares for and plays the 2016 match against Go champion Lee Sedol. It covers the team, the games, and the emotional reaction of the Go world to an AI beating a top human.
WXuK6gekU1Y.quote: I consider AlphaGo - The Movie [1] to be a timeless classic that will never feel outdated.

WXuK6gekU1Y: AlphaGo: the full documentary of DeepMind's match against Lee Sedol.
wjZofJX0v4M: HN treats it as the go-to visual introduction to transformers, and many say it finally made attention and embeddings click.

wjZofJX0v4M.summary: 3Blue1Brown's visual explanation of how transformers and GPT-style language models work, tracing data through tokens, embeddings and attention.
wjZofJX0v4M.quote: what bade me finally understand the transformer architecture [0] and attention [1], are 3Blue1Brown's videos.

ajGX7odA87k: HN considers it a classic, hilarious and sobering talk on ML inscrutability and tech hubris, often rewatched.

ajGX7odA87k.summary: James Mickens's humorous USENIX Security keynote argues that improving security and trusting opaque technology like machine learning is far harder than the industry admits.
ajGX7odA87k.quote: His keynote at USENIX Security 2018 is by far the best summation of the dangers of ML that I've ever seen.

UzxYlbK2c7E: Recommended as the rigorous, math-heavy original course, deeper than the Coursera version, for learning machine learning.

UzxYlbK2c7E.summary: The first lecture of Andrew Ng's Stanford CS229 Machine Learning course, giving an overview of the course. It introduces supervised and unsupervised learning, learning theory and reinforcement learning.
UzxYlbK2c7E.quote: I'd suggest going back to the original youtube[1] and course materials[2].

7xTGNNLPyMI: HN's most frequent recommendation for a clear, approachable foundation in how LLMs work without heavy math.

7xTGNNLPyMI.summary: Andrej Karpathy's three-hour-plus general-audience deep dive into how ChatGPT-style LLMs are built, covering the full training stack from pretraining to post-training. It also gives mental models for their quirks, like hallucination, and how to use them well.
7xTGNNLPyMI.quote: I highly recommend Andrej Karpathy's Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT

WUvTyaaNkzM: A staple recommendation for anyone learning math, praised for visual intuition that makes memorized formulas make sense.

WUvTyaaNkzM.summary: The first video of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Calculus series, which builds toward integrals, derivatives, and the fundamental theorem of calculus from a simple geometry question. It aims to make viewers feel they could have invented calculus themselves.
WUvTyaaNkzM.quote: When I discovered that video, all the formulas they tried to make me memorize started making a LOT more sense.

2pWv7GOvuf0: Frequently recommended as an excellent, clear introductory RL course from the lead of AlphaGo, pairing well with Sutton and Barto.

2pWv7GOvuf0.summary: The first lecture of David Silver's reinforcement learning course, introducing the field and its basic concepts. The course follows the Sutton and Barto textbook.
2pWv7GOvuf0.quote: Really clear explanations that went hand in hand when I was reading Sutton and Barto's introductory book.

kCc8FmEb1nY: It is the go-to recommendation for learning how transformers and LLMs actually work, praised for its clarity and Karpathy's teaching.

kCc8FmEb1nY.summary: Andrej Karpathy builds a GPT from scratch in code, following Attention Is All You Need and GPT-2/3, in about two hours using PyTorch. He connects it to ChatGPT and assumes familiarity with his earlier makemore videos.
kCc8FmEb1nY.quote: the best video I have seen on the topic

ZmNOAtZIgIk: HN commenters recommended it for years as a simple, exciting overview of the deep learning wave.

ZmNOAtZIgIk.summary: Andrew Ng presents unsupervised feature learning and deep learning, showing how algorithms can learn representations from unlabeled data instead of hand-designed features. He gives examples in vision and audio, including visualizations of features learned by successive layers.
ZmNOAtZIgIk.quote: he explains very simply how all this works for images and some examples about the audio case.

jkrNMKz9pWU: Repeatedly named the best practical tutorial for using LLMs, with a well-liked fine-tuning section.

jkrNMKz9pWU.summary: Jeremy Howard's 90-minute practical tour of language models. It covers how they work, GPT-4's capabilities and limits, using the OpenAI API, code writing, data analysis and fine-tuning.
jkrNMKz9pWU.quote: highly recommend "Hackers Guide to language models" by Jeremy Howard. 1.5h video packed with practical information

kjBOesZCoqc: HN repeatedly recommends the series as the best intuition-first, visual introduction to linear algebra and a benchmark for clear math explanation.

kjBOesZCoqc.summary: A five-minute preview of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Linear Algebra series, which uses animation to build geometric intuition for topics from a standard linear algebra course.
kjBOesZCoqc.quote: 3Blue1Brown's youtube series I cannot recommend highly enough.

ZeecOKBus3Q: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it as the clearest introduction to why smart AI might behave badly by default.

ZeecOKBus3Q.summary: Robert Miles explains instrumental convergence: why an AGI with almost any goal would tend to pursue sub-goals like self-preservation and resource acquisition. It builds on Omohundro's basic AI drives and his orthogonality thesis video.
ZeecOKBus3Q.quote: Robert Miles' videos are among the best presented arguments about specific points in this list

hx7BXih7zx8: HN repeatedly points to it as the best public technical overview of Tesla's FSD approach, used both to defend and to critique Tesla's progress.

hx7BXih7zx8.summary: Andrej Karpathy, then Tesla's head of AI, presents at ScaledML 2020 on how Tesla builds full self-driving using vision-based neural nets and fleet data collection. He covers training custom detectors and neural nets gradually replacing traditional code.
hx7BXih7zx8.quote: I highly recommend watching head of AI at Tesla Andrej Karpathy's talk on their self driving architecture.

zjkBMFhNj_g: HN recommends it as the dense, approachable starting point for understanding LLMs and often cites it for specific claims about scaling and training.

zjkBMFhNj_g.summary: Andrej Karpathy gives a one-hour general-audience introduction to large language models, covering what they are, how they are trained, comparisons to operating systems, and security challenges such as jailbreaks.
zjkBMFhNj_g.quote: Start with his short intro to LLMs, only 1 hour long but is dense with valuable stuff

0xS68sl2D70: Recommended as a balanced take on AI and education, with the point that learning takes work that no technology can do for you.

0xS68sl2D70.summary: Veritasium's Derek Muller gives a Perimeter Institute livestream on how AI might change teaching and learning. He draws on past technology shifts and cognitive science to argue that learning requires effortful repetition.
0xS68sl2D70.quote: I think the best take on that I've seen so far was from Derek (Veritasium) in this recent talk

P-2P3MSZrBM: Praised as a long but rewarding conversation, with commenters especially liking Bach's emphasis on modelling as a skill and his bridge between mind and computation.

P-2P3MSZrBM.summary: Lex Fridman has a three-hour conversation with Joscha Bach about artificial consciousness, the workings of the mind, intelligence and the possibly simulated nature of reality.
P-2P3MSZrBM.quote: If watching this isn't worth anyone's time, I'm not sure what would be.

hEUO6pjwFOo: HN people use it as the standard short explanation for why AI can understand human ethics without sharing them, and often recommend the whole channel.

hEUO6pjwFOo.summary: Robert Miles explains the orthogonality thesis: how an agent can be highly intelligent while pursuing goals that seem stupid or alien to humans. He separates intelligence from goals and touches on the stamp-collector example.
hEUO6pjwFOo.quote: this video to me states the problem in a nutshell (that whole channel is gold)

vq2nnJ4g6N0: Repeatedly called an excellent, practical introduction that covers a lot in two hours and explains issues academic textbooks skip.

vq2nnJ4g6N0.summary: Martin Gorner's Devoxx talk introduces deep learning with TensorFlow, walking through neural networks for MNIST, how to choose an architecture and how to diagnose networks that fail to train.
vq2nnJ4g6N0.quote: Tensorflow and deep learning - without a PhD" is really good, and covers a lot of material in a single 2hr talk.

DleXA5ADG78: Recommended as a simple, elegant explanation of dropout and its connection to how the brain works.

DleXA5ADG78.summary: Geoffrey Hinton's Google Tech Talk linking machine learning to biology, explaining dropout as a form of model averaging and why sexual reproduction and stochastic spiking neurons may prevent overfitting.
DleXA5ADG78.quote: If you want a great overview of the dropout technique, watch this tech talk by Hinton

kTiP0zKF9bc: The go-to link in any anti-cheat thread for a concrete, well-delivered account of machine-learning cheat detection in production.

kTiP0zKF9bc.summary: Valve's John McDonald presents at GDC 2018 on how Valve uses deep learning (VACnet) to detect cheaters in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. He covers training on human-reviewed replays and how model output is confirmed by manual review.
kTiP0zKF9bc.quote: The presenter delivered the problem and solution approach so well I'd still like to work on something like this some time.

lhYGXYeMq_E: Recommended to people who find it inspiring or perspective-changing on pursuing goals, open-ended search and AI beyond optimization.

lhYGXYeMq_E.summary: A long Machine Learning Street Talk interview with Kenneth Stanley, creator of NEAT and novelty search, about his book on why greatness cannot be planned. They discuss open-endedness, the tyranny of objectives, serendipity and the evolution of ideas.
lhYGXYeMq_E.quote: It really changed my perspective on achieving my long term goals

mbyG85GZ0PI: Recommended repeatedly in 'where do I start with ML' threads as a clear, math-aware introduction.

mbyG85GZ0PI.summary: The first lecture of Caltech's CS 156 Machine Learning course by Yaser Abu-Mostafa, introducing the learning problem and supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. It is one of 18 lectures in the Learning from Data course.
mbyG85GZ0PI.quote: I have found the Caltech machine learning intro course to be the most elucidating of any resource so far

GVsUOuSjvcg: Treated as the accessible reference on analog computing for neural nets, especially the Mythic AI segment.

GVsUOuSjvcg.summary: Veritasium explains why analog computing may suit AI workloads, covering old analog computers, The Analog Thing and Mythic's analog chips that use flash memory for neural network inference. It argues digital hardware is hitting limits.
GVsUOuSjvcg.quote: Veritasium explains it really well in general here (and demos the device)

pYXy-A4siMw: The default link for newcomers wanting an approachable, entertaining introduction to AI risk and alignment.

pYXy-A4siMw.summary: Robert Miles gives a remastered introduction to AI safety, adapted from a talk in London. It lays out why advanced AI could go wrong and answers common objections.
pYXy-A4siMw.quote: It's quite an approachable intro, often entertaining

qbIk7-JPB2c: HN recommends it as a thought-provoking talk from a researcher with early GPT-4 access, especially for the unicorn degrading under safety tuning.

qbIk7-JPB2c.summary: Sebastien Bubeck presents the Sparks of AGI paper at MIT, showing early experiments with GPT-4 across many domains and asking whether artificial intelligence has arrived. It includes the TikZ unicorn example.
qbIk7-JPB2c.quote: Highly highly highly recommend listen to this lecture by Sebastien Bubeck

zduSFxRajkE: Recommended as the best deep dive on tokenizers, worth the two hours for anyone working with LLMs.

zduSFxRajkE.summary: Andrej Karpathy builds the GPT tokenizer from scratch, implementing byte pair encoding along with encode and decode. He shows how many odd LLM behaviors trace back to tokenization, and covers Unicode byte encodings along the way.
zduSFxRajkE.quote: Worth spending 2h for the deeper understanding if you deal with LLMs.

L5pUA3LsEaw: HN points to it as an accessible rebuttal to the claim that AI risk is just corporate risk.

L5pUA3LsEaw.summary: Robert Miles asks whether corporations can be thought of as artificial general superintelligences and how far the analogy holds. He argues the differences, such as being limited by employees' capabilities, matter for AI safety.
L5pUA3LsEaw.quote: He presents the material in a very interesting and accessible way.

MFRWDuduuSw: HN recommends Herb Gross as an unusually clear teacher whose explanations make calculus click for people who struggled elsewhere.

MFRWDuduuSw.summary: The preface to Herb Gross's MIT OpenCourseWare 'Calculus Revisited: Single Variable Calculus', an older black-and-white lecture series. It introduces his approach to teaching calculus from the basics.
MFRWDuduuSw.quote: The way he explains things just clicked, after numerous failed attempts to learn from other sources.

cKxRvEZd3Mw: HN commenters recommend it as an approachable first step into machine learning for programmers, with an apples-vs-oranges classifier.

cKxRvEZd3Mw.quote: Very approachable! The first lesson is a classifier to separate apples and oranges.

eMlx5fFNoYc: HN treats it as the go-to visual explanation of attention, recommended to people who find text-based transformer explainers hard to follow.

eMlx5fFNoYc.summary: 3Blue1Brown's visual walkthrough of the attention mechanism inside transformers, covering self-attention, multiple heads and cross-attention. It is chapter 6 of his deep learning series.
eMlx5fFNoYc.quote: what bade me finally understand the transformer architecture [0] and attention [1], are 3Blue1Brown's videos.

eMlx5fFNoYc: Explains Attention Is All You Need

ObhK8lUfIlc: HN points to it as the definitive example of server-side, behavioral, non-invasive anti-cheat using machine learning, often as a counterpoint to kernel-level anti-cheat.

S27pHKBEp30: Recommended as a clear explanation of why RNNs fall short and how transformers solve it.

S27pHKBEp30.summary: Leo Dirac explains how transformer models have replaced LSTMs in NLP. He gives background from bag of words through RNNs and LSTMs, then a technical deep dive into multi-headed self-attention and positional encoding, with sample code.
S27pHKBEp30.quote: has gotten tons of compliments and keeps people watching year after year

_L3gNaAVjQ4: Commenters recommend it as an entertaining, wide-ranging interview, and cite it for Hotz's views on end-to-end neural-net driving.

_L3gNaAVjQ4.quote: Lots of topics covered: self-driving, immortality, UFOs, cryptocurrencies, Tesla/Waymo/OpenAI, GTP-3, AI, book recommendations.

iDulhoQ2pro: HN recommends it as an accessible, clear walkthrough of the transformer paper for people with some AI background.

iDulhoQ2pro: Explains Attention Is All You Need

iDulhoQ2pro.why: Yannic Kilcher's read-through of the Transformer paper.

ne99laPUxN4: Cited as the more accessible companion to the paper, and as the most interesting treatment of AD via compiling to categories.

Varying the representation of derivatives yields forward and reverse mode algorithms that avoid the complexity and statefulness of backpropagation.
ne99laPUxN4.quote: There's a talk that Conal gives that makes the paper a bit more accessible

Ilg3gGewQ5U: Recommended as the most accessible introduction to backprop for people who struggle with the pure math.

Ilg3gGewQ5U.summary: 3Blue1Brown's third deep learning chapter gives a visual, intuitive account of backpropagation and what happens to a neural network as it learns. A follow-up video covers the underlying calculus.
Ilg3gGewQ5U.quote: I found the explainations by 3Brown1Blue to be very intuitive when it comes to neural networks

JRuNA2eK7w0: HN points to it as a reasoned rebuttal to the claim that AI risk is just Pascal's wager.

JRuNA2eK7w0.summary: Robert Miles examines whether the case for AI safety is a Pascal's mugging, a tiny probability of an enormous payoff. He argues it is not, because AI risk does not depend on vanishingly small probabilities.
JRuNA2eK7w0.quote: the main point of the video is that kind of situation happens when the probability involved is vanishingly small

PYylPRX6z4Q: Seen as the clearest introduction to the idea behind RLHF, and also borrowed by commenters as a metaphor for human motivation.

PYylPRX6z4Q.quote: I find this video by Rob Miles still the best presentation of the ingenious original 2017(!) paper

Qi1Yry33TQE: HN points to it as the sharpest, most-quoted critique of deep learning practice, and cites it whenever ML reliability or understanding is debated.

Qi1Yry33TQE.quote: For a more cutting and insightful critique, watch Ali Rahimi's short talk at NIPS 2017

5MdSE-N0bxs: HN recommends it as a clear argument for why deep and cheap learning succeeds, often alongside the associated paper.

5MdSE-N0bxs.summary: Max Tegmark's MIT CBMM talk on why deep learning works so well. He argues that the laws of physics and the symmetries in physical data make it compressible into small neural networks, tying physics to network structure.
5MdSE-N0bxs.quote: physical data tends to have symmetries, and these symmetries make descriptions of the data very compressible into relatively small neural circuits

IHZwWFHWa-w: HN recommends the series as a very accessible way to understand the math behind machine learning and LLMs.

IHZwWFHWa-w.summary: 3Blue1Brown's second neural network chapter explains cost functions and gradient descent, showing how a network learns by minimizing error during training.
IHZwWFHWa-w.quote: 3Blue1Brown which explains math in very accessible way

IkdziSLYzHw: HN readers recommend it as an intuitive explanation of neural networks that shifts how people think about AI and language.

IkdziSLYzHw.summary: Geoffrey Hinton's 2025 Royal Institution Discourse on what AI has learned from biological intelligence and how it might surpass it. He explains neural networks and argues that human language use resembles what backpropagation-trained networks do.
IkdziSLYzHw.quote: Richard Sutton takes a different view in an interview with Dwarkesh Patel[2]

IxuU5L2MEII: HN commenters point to it as a candid, contrarian view of self-driving approaches and the real limits of the business.

IxuU5L2MEII.summary: George Hotz of Comma AI gives a 2017 conference talk on lessons from building a self-driving system. He argues about how driving should be defined and why the common approach to autonomous vehicles is flawed.
IxuU5L2MEII.quote: George Hotz has a killer talk about why the general approach to autonomous vehicles is flawed. I highly recommend it.

OQQ-W_63UgQ: Recommended as one of the best free courses for learning modern deep learning for NLP.

OQQ-W_63UgQ.summary: The first lecture of Stanford's Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning course, taught by Chris Manning and Richard Socher. It introduces NLP and word vectors, including SVD, skip-gram, CBOW, negative sampling and word2vec.
OQQ-W_63UgQ.quote: I will suggest two brilliant courses from Stanford

bZQun8Y4L2A: Recommended as the clearest overview of how LLM assistants are built and how to use them well.

bZQun8Y4L2A.summary: Andrej Karpathy walks through how GPT assistants are trained, from tokenization and pretraining to supervised finetuning and RLHF, and gives practical prompting strategies and a view of the tooling ecosystem.
bZQun8Y4L2A.quote: It changed the way I use GPT-4.

bxe2T-V8XRs: HN commenters point beginners to this series as one of the clearest short walkthroughs of how neural networks and backpropagation work.

bxe2T-V8XRs.summary: The first of a short series by Welch Labs on building a complete neural network in Python. It introduces the data and the architecture of a simple network before later parts cover forward propagation, gradient descent, and backpropagation.
bxe2T-V8XRs.quote: One of the clearest walkthroughs I've seen online is a short series of very short videos by Stephen C Welch [2] [3].

cdiD-9MMpb0: Cited for Karpathy's first-hand explanations of camera-only self-driving, transformers and ML trends.

cdiD-9MMpb0.summary: Lex Fridman's long conversation with Andrej Karpathy on Tesla's self-driving approach, Optimus, neural networks, transformers, AGI and more. It also touches on his OpenAI work and working with Elon Musk.
cdiD-9MMpb0.quote: Anyone seriously interested in this question should listen to the Lex Friedman interview of Andrej Karpathy

dKJEpOtVgXc: HN commenters recommend it for building intuition about state space models and the tradeoffs between transformer and SSM layers.

dKJEpOtVgXc.quote: I highly recommend Sasha Rush's video on it

e3K5UxWRRuY: HN commenters call it lucid and fluff-free, and point to Bach as one of the most interesting voices on AI, consciousness and philosophy.

e3K5UxWRRuY.summary: Joscha Bach's 35C3 talk offers an AI perspective on the soul, covering perception, mental representation, agency, consciousness and selfhood as things that can arise in a computational system like the brain.
e3K5UxWRRuY.quote: the whole talk is incredibly lucid and contains zero fluff or BS

g6bOwQdCJrc: HN commenters cite it in Tesla threads as the primary-source explanation of why Tesla removed radar and how its vision depth estimation works.

g6bOwQdCJrc.summary: Andrej Karpathy, then Tesla's head of AI, gives a CVPR 2021 workshop keynote on how Autopilot's neural networks work. A large part covers the move to a vision-only stack, including why radar was dropped and how vision produces depth estimates.
g6bOwQdCJrc.quote: This talk was worth watching (any Karpathy or Carmack talk is imo)

nU8DcBF-qo4: HN recommends it as the clear explanation of why Google's statistical, data-first approach works.

nU8DcBF-qo4.quote: You should definitely watch it if you haven't seen it before.

yvDCzhbjYWs: Recommended as a favorite tech talk showing how huge data availability changes how problems are approached.

yvDCzhbjYWs.summary: Peter Norvig's UBC distinguished lecture on how massive amounts of simple data, such as for language modeling, can yield understanding that hand-built models could not.
yvDCzhbjYWs.quote: Norvig does an especially great job in making you truly appreciate the seismic impact that the availability of massive quantities of data can have

BCiZc0n6COY: Recommended as an enjoyable, clear introduction to information theory that pairs well with MacKay's free textbook.

G4hL5Om4IJ4: Recommended as a stellar long-form interview with someone both very smart and wise, mined for CPU design insights.

G4hL5Om4IJ4.quote: Investing time to listen to the guy seems to be not worse.

Gh-Tff7DdzU: HN points to it as a technical talk from a chip designer on why AI hardware should put memory close to compute and use async data transfers.

Gh-Tff7DdzU.quote: Here's a nice technical talk from Graphcore's CTO about that

I845O57ZSy4: HN mines it for Carmack's views on AGI, debuggers, tooling and the metaverse, and recommends it as worth the full length.

I845O57ZSy4.summary: A five-hour Lex Fridman interview with John Carmack covering Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, programming, games and rockets.
I845O57ZSy4.quote: The entire video is worth viewing, an impressive 5:15h!

OyFJWRnt_AY: HN recommends it to newcomers as a clear explanation of attention, including the query/key/value intuition.

Ucp0TTmvqOE: Cited both as a primary source on Tesla's technical autonomy approach and, later, for Musk's unmet robotaxi predictions.

Ucp0TTmvqOE.summary: Tesla's roughly four-hour Autonomy Day investor event covers its in-house self-driving chip, vision-only approach, fleet data engine and robotaxi plans, with talks by Andrej Karpathy and others.

VkIJbpdTujE: HN recommends it as an accessible introduction to Gaussian splats, made by people who understand the subject.

XxCha4Kez9c: Recommended in address and OCR threads as a look at the last human mail-coding operation.

lnA9DMvHtfI: HN recommends it as a quick, non-dumbed-down way to get up to speed on how LLMs are built.

pdJQ8iVTwj8: HN points to it as the main place to hear Lattner's motivations and design ideas for Mojo, often in Mojo threads.

rURRYI66E54: Pointed to as an accessible early explanation of transformers and attention for newcomers.

-EVqrDlAqYo: HN people send others here to hear Hawkins explain his theory in his own words, including reference frames and the old versus new brain.

ODSJsviD_SU: HN uses it as primary-source evidence on how Tesla's vision-based driving stack and training pipeline work.

P_fHJIYENdI: HN points to it as an accessible explainer of AlphaFold and as an example of narrow, specialized ML delivering real scientific breakthroughs.

QPgqfnKG_T4: HN loves it as a funny, inspiring hobby project and calls it one of the best conference talks ever.

YXylqtEQ0tk: HN recommends it as a technical talk aimed at a real engineering audience, with live demos of perception and pre-mapped roads.

lFXJWPhDsSY: HN recommends it as a striking, well-explained example of AlphaZero's play and of zugzwang.

lqJUIqZNzP8: HN recommends Robert Miles' channel as a clear starting point for people curious about AI safety.

rsxCZAE8QNA: HN points to it for an insider view of why NVIDIA's AI gains came from design rather than process, and for data-movement power costs.

160F8F8mXlo: HN treats it as the origin of the full-wine-glass meme and an illustration of how models lack concepts missing from their training data.

21EiKfQYZXc: Recommended as a broad, practical view of AI's near-term impact from a leading practitioner, with his argument that worrying about evil AI is premature.

3TYT1QfdfsM: HN points to it as the standard response to the argument that we can just unplug a dangerous AI.

3wMKoSRbGVs: Pointed to as the long-form interview for understanding Lenat's work, especially after his death.

5eqRuVp65eY: Recommended as a well-made, digestible introduction to scaling laws and why models cluster along a similar efficiency frontier.

7PKx3kS7f4A: Pointed to in AI safety debates as a short explanation of why encoding human values as simple rules is so hard.

9i1WlcCudpU: HN commenters link it as a compact rebuttal to dismissive arguments and as a way to see why people consider AI safety important.

LNjJTgXujno: HN points to it as a source for Norvig's 'unreasonable effectiveness of data' argument and for his views on image search and the semantic web.

QWWgr2rN45o: HN recommends it for Hinton's research history and the two pioneers reflecting on a decade of progress.
